result.detailed_feedback:
**Element Layout (18.5 points):**
The video utilizes a highly effective split-screen layout: instructional text on the left and supporting animations on the right. This dual-coding approach manages cognitive load well. Headings are clear and consistently placed. The 'BINS' criteria section uses spatial organization effectively to associate letters with visual symbols (lightbulbs). However, the text on the left could benefit from slightly more varied typography to emphasize key terms beyond simple color changes.

**Attractiveness (17.5 points):**
The aesthetic is clean and professional, using a high-contrast black background that makes colors like green (success) and red (failure) pop. The 'Lucky the Squirrel' character provides a friendly, low-stakes entry point into a complex mathematical topic. The dynamic histogram is particularly attractive as it shifts in real-time, providing an engaging visual representation of data variance.

**Logic Flow (19.0 points):**
The pedagogical progression is excellent. It starts with the fundamental building block (Bernoulli Trial), moves to the necessary conditions (BINS), introduces the mathematical formula, visualizes the distribution (Histogram), and concludes with a practical calculation. Each step logically builds upon the previous one, facilitating a deep understanding of why the distribution behaves the way it does.

**Accuracy & Depth (19.5 points):**
The content is mathematically rigorous and highly accurate. Using the BINS mnemonic is standard educational practice for this knowledge point. The deconstruction of the binomial formula is particularly strong, as it explains the 'why' behind each component (combinations, success probability, and failure probability). The visualization of how 'p' affects skewness is a sophisticated touch that adds depth beyond basic calculation.

**Visual Consistency (19.0 points):**
Visual standards are maintained throughout. There is a consistent color language: green for 'p' (success) and red for '1-p' (failure), which is carried through the squirrel animation, the formula, and the histogram. The timing between the text appearing on the left and the corresponding animation on the right is perfectly synchronized, creating a seamless learning experience.

**Overall Summary:**
This is an exceptional educational video on Binomial Distributions. It successfully bridges the gap between abstract probability formulas and visual intuition. The use of 'Lucky the Squirrel' serves as a great mnemonic for the Bernoulli trial, while the dynamic histogram effectively teaches the impact of probability shifts on distribution shape. The 'BINS' section is a standout for pedagogical clarity.

**Key Strengths:**
• Perfect use of the BINS mnemonic to teach requirements.
• Excellent color-coding (Green/Red) consistently applied to success/failure concepts.
• Dynamic histogram effectively demonstrates the relationship between 'p' and skewness.
• Clear deconstruction of the binomial probability formula parts.

**Areas for Improvement:**
• The section on 'n-choose-k' could use a brief visual example of a combination to help students understand the 'ways to arrange' concept more deeply.
• Slightly increase the font size of the sub-text on the left to ensure readability on smaller mobile devices.
• The final slide on 'Real-World Application' is a bit brief; a concrete 5-second example of a specific risk (e.g., component failure in engineering) would solidify the concept.

B
A binomial distribution models the probability of a specific number of "successes" (k) occurring in a fixed number of independent trials (n), where each trial has the same two possible outcomes and the same probability of success.

C
A Bernoulli trial is a random experiment that has exactly two possible outcomes, which are conventionally labeled "success" and "failure."

C
The center (mean) of a binomial distribution is calculated as n*p, and the width (standard deviation) is the square root of n*p*(1-p). Since both parameters, n (number of trials) and p (probability of success), are in both formulas, changing either one will alter both the center and the width of the graph.

B
This is the binomial probability formula. It is composed of three parts: C(n, k), the number of combinations (ways to choose k successes from n trials); p^k, the probability of k successes; and (1-p)^{n-k}, the probability of n-k failures.

C
When the probability of success `p` is low (e.g., 0.1), successes are rare. Therefore, even with a large number of trials `n`, the most probable outcomes will be a small number of successes. This concentrates the bulk of the probability mass at low values, creating a peak on the left and a long tail extending to the right.
